fluff.overview: The Olympus Recharge Station is the largest and most capable space station class still operating at the nadir and zenith jump points of inhabited star systems across the Inner Sphere. Commissioned in 2663 through Di Tron Heavy Industries, the class was designed to give the Star League Defense Force a permanent, distributed infrastructure for sustaining JumpShip operations across its vast network of garrisoned worlds. At just over one million tons and 1,500 meters in diameter, the Olympus dwarfed earlier recharge platforms and established a logistical standard that no subsequent design has matched. Beyond its primary role recharging JumpShip drives, the class serves as a repair depot, cargo transfer point, and early-warning sensor platform, making a fully operational Olympus one of the most strategically valuable fixed installations a star system can possess. The design remains in limited active service despite centuries of attrition, a reflection of the scale and quality of original Star League construction programs.
fluff.capabilities:
The Olympus is built around three pressurized Naval Repair Facilities, each rated for vessels up to 50,000 tons, enabling simultaneous servicing of multiple DropShips in fully enclosed, pressure-controlled environments. These bays operate at consistently high utilization wherever the station is functional, and obtaining a berth can require advance booking of six months or more. Four docking collars allow continued vessel traffic during repair operations. A single cargo bay with twelve access doors holds nearly 944,000 tons of stores, fuel, spare components, and consumables, supporting extended independent logistics operations without resupply from a planetary base. Six small craft and six aerospace fighters operate from dedicated bays with two recovery positions each, providing security, courier, and escort services for both station personnel and visiting vessels.

The station's complement of 46 officers, 263 enlisted crew, and 22 gunners, along with any embarked passengers, are housed on two grav decks. The primary deck, at 1,230 meters in diameter, is the largest gravitational habitability structure ever built in the Inner Sphere and holds all passenger and crew quarters. A smaller 150-meter secondary deck supports operational overflow and specialized station functions. Fifty escape pods and fifteen life boats provide emergency coverage for all personnel aboard.

Eight solar energy-collection banks allow the Olympus to deliver a rapid charge to a JumpShip's Kearny-Fuchida drive through either microwave transmission or direct cable connection, significantly reducing recharge time compared to passive solar collection. Defensively, the station mounts an identical weapon battery across all six firing arcs (combining particle projector cannons, long-range missile racks, autocannons, and laser systems) to eliminate blind spots in its coverage. This uniform arc configuration means no approach vector offers an undefended avenue of attack. Two hundred heat sinks provide thermal management for defensive engagements. The station cannot maneuver and presents a fixed target; its defenses are sufficient to deter raider-scale threats but offer little resilience against warship-level assault, and no capacity exists to withdraw from danger.
fluff.deployment: The 3072 configuration reflects Inner Sphere advanced-technology upgrades applied to surviving Olympus stations during the Jihad period. Original weapons are replaced throughout with extended-range and improved systems including ER PPCs, Gauss Rifles, and MML-9 launchers with Artemis IV fire control, while small laser batteries give way to laser-based anti-missile systems across all arcs. Double heat sinks replace the original single installation. The gunner complement is reduced to fourteen compared to twenty-two in the base configuration, likely reflecting the more automated nature of the upgraded weapon systems and the anti-missile defense network. Passenger capacity of 126 is retained, consistent with the station's dual role as repair facility and regional administrative hub. This configuration most plausibly represents stations upgraded by Successor State technical programs responding to the elevated threat environment of the Jihad, when surviving recharge stations became both more critical to interstellar logistics and more valuable as military targets.
fluff.history:
Di Tron Heavy Industries developed the Olympus design to meet SLDF logistics requirements that smaller or improvised recharge platforms could not adequately satisfy. Early Star League naval planning had relied on a patchwork of older stations and temporary facilities, a situation that proved increasingly inadequate as the SLDF extended its operational reach toward the Periphery border regions. Construction of the first stations began following the design's commissioning in 2663, with facilities sited at the jump points of industrial worlds, garrison staging systems, and high-volume trade corridors. By the height of the Star League era, the class was deployed across hundreds of systems; in principle, one at each of the nadir and zenith jump points of every important system in the Inner Sphere, and many less critical ones as well.

The stations served both military and commercial traffic, and their combination of JumpShip recharging, DropShip repair, and cargo handling made them as much commercial hubs as military installations. Their dual-use character contributed to their political neutrality during the early Succession Wars; attacking forces on both sides recognized that destroying an Olympus denied them a facility they themselves would need. This unspoken pragmatism kept many stations intact through the initial campaigns of the First Succession War, though covert neutralization of sensor and communications systems was a common alternative - a way to blind a station's early-warning capabilities without eliminating its recharging utility.

When the Star League collapsed and the SLDF departed with Kerensky, Olympus stations passed under the authority of whatever Successor State or local power controlled the systems they occupied. Many became contested assets immediately, recognized as force multipliers for any faction trying to maintain aging JumpShip fleets without Star League-era construction capacity. Individual stations were captured and recaptured as transit corridors shifted, and the growing intensity of the Succession Wars eventually eroded the informal protection that strategic pragmatism had provided. Stations located along contested routes were destroyed in naval engagements, progressively cannibalized for components needed elsewhere, or simply abandoned when the technical expertise required to maintain them could no longer be found. Several survived centuries through a combination of favorable geography, neutral status, and the dedication of local technical communities that sustained aging systems through improvised maintenance and component substitution.

By the late twenty-eighth century, fully operational examples had become rare enough to represent significant regional strategic assets. Individual surviving stations became targets of political and military intrigue. A station at the zenith jump point of the New Syrtis system was briefly seized by pro-Steiner forces in 3065 during fighting on that world, while a station at the Kaifeng jump point was captured by Capellan forces in 3058 as part of a covert operation to facilitate an invasion, its sensor communications disabled to prevent warning traffic from reaching the planet below. DCMS aerospace elements based at surviving stations (including those at Dieron) used them as fixed platforms for system-defense operations into the post-Star League period, demonstrating that even degraded examples retained meaningful tactical value. These episodes illustrate how surviving stations had become both prizes and operational tools for factions sophisticated enough to exploit them.

No new production of the Olympus class is known to have been initiated since the fall of the Star League. Di Tron Heavy Industries' role as constructor is documented in surviving Star League records, but no production facilities or replacement programs have been identified in the centuries since. Surviving stations continue to operate on the strength of their original construction quality and the resourcefulness of their caretaker communities, their numbers diminishing gradually with each decade of losses to combat, accident, and irreparable mechanical failure.
